paragraphs.context: Fired with a housewifely wish to see her storeroom stocked with homemade preserves
paragraphs.mainIdea: Meg tries to make currant jelly like Hannah. She works all day, but the jelly will not set.
paragraphs.simple: Meg wished very much to see her storeroom full of jelly and fruit she had made herself. So she decided to make her own currant jelly. John was asked to send home a dozen little pots and extra sugar, because their own currants were ripe and had to be dealt with at once. John firmly believed his wife could do anything, and he was proud of her skill. He wanted her to be pleased and to save their only crop of fruit for winter. Home came four dozen little pots, half a barrel of sugar, and a small boy to pick the currants. Meg tucked her hair into a cap, bared her arms to the elbow, and put on a checked apron. She began work sure of success, because she had seen Hannah do it hundreds of times. The many pots surprised her, but John loved jelly and the jars would look nice on the top shelf, so she decided to fill them all. She spent a long day picking, boiling, straining and fussing. She did her best, asked Mrs. Cornelius for advice, and tried to remember what Hannah did. She boiled and sugared it again, but that dreadful stuff would not 'jell'.

paragraphs.context: Next day she put her pride in her pocket, went to Sallie, told the truth
paragraphs.mainIdea: Meg asks Sallie to buy the silk dress. She gives John the greatcoat he needs, and the two are happy again.
paragraphs.simple: The next day Meg put her pride away, went to Sallie, told her the truth, and asked her as a favor to buy the silk. Good-natured Mrs. Moffat did so, and was kind enough not to give it to Meg as a gift soon after. Then Meg ordered the greatcoat home. When John came, she put it on and asked how he liked her new silk gown. You can guess his answer and how he took his present. John came home early, Meg did not go out and about any more, and the greatcoat was put on each morning by a very happy husband and taken off each night by a loving little wife. So the year went round, and at midsummer Meg had a new experience, the deepest and gentlest in a woman's life.

sentences.context: John Brooke laughed then as he never dared to laugh afterward
sentences.simple: John laughed then in a way that he never dared to laugh again.
sentences.grammar: 'As he never dared to laugh afterward' is a comparison clause. It tells us the laugh was a big one, and that John later learned it was unwise.

sentences.context: for even turtledoves will peck when ruffled
sentences.simple: Even gentle doves will peck when they are upset.
sentences.grammar: 'For' gives a reason. 'When ruffled' is short for 'when they are ruffled'. It means that even loving people can become sharp.

sentences.context: It always happens so in this vale of tears
sentences.simple: Things always happen like this in this sad world.
sentences.grammar: 'Vale of tears' is an old name for life on earth, full of sorrow. The writer uses it in a funny way for a small trouble.
